questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: classify a measured diagonal as rational or irrational
questions.stem: A flooring contractor records the diagonal of a 1 metre by 1 metre tile as exactly 1.41421356 metres. Which statement about the true diagonal is correct?

options.text: It is rational because the contractor wrote a finite decimal for it
options.misconception: believes writing a rounded decimal makes an irrational value rational

options.text: It is irrational because no fraction of integers equals the exact diagonal
It is rational because every length a ruler can measure must be rational
options.misconception: believes physical measurability forces a number to be rational

options.text: It is neither rational nor irrational because it cannot be written exactly
options.misconception: believes some real numbers are outside both the rational and irrational sets

questions.explanation: The exact diagonal is the square root of 2, and there is no fraction of integers whose square equals 2, so the value is irrational. The written decimal is only a rounded stand-in for it; a finite decimal is one way of writing a rational number, and this length has no finite exact decimal. Every real number is exactly one of rational or irrational, so option D describes an impossible category.
questions.hint: Ask whether a fraction with whole-number top and bottom can equal the exact length.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: sort mixed numbers into rational and irrational bins
questions.stem: A student sorts the numbers 0.272727..., the fraction 3 over 8, the square root of 49, and the square root of 7 into bins. Which one belongs in the irrational bin?

options.text: The square root of 7, because no fraction of whole numbers squares to 7
The fraction 3 over 8, because the top is smaller than the bottom
options.misconception: believes a proper fraction hides an irrational value somewhere

options.text: The square root of 49, because 49 is not a perfect square
options.misconception: believes 49 has no whole-number square root

options.text: 0.272727 with the block 27 repeating, because its digits never run out
options.misconception: believes a decimal that never ends cannot be written as a fraction

questions.explanation: The decimal 0.272727... is 27 over 99, which reduces to 3 over 11, so it is rational; a repeating block is the signature of a rational number rather than an irrational one. The fraction 3 over 8 is rational by definition. The square root of 49 equals 7 exactly, since 7 squared is 49. The square root of 7 has no fraction equal to it, because 7 is not a perfect square, so it alone is irrational.
questions.hint: Try to rewrite each number as a fraction with whole-number parts.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: apply the closure rule for rational plus irrational
questions.stem: A baker writes a total of 5 plus an irrational number t. Which claim about that total is guaranteed no matter which irrational t is chosen?

options.text: The total is rational whenever t happens to be negative
options.misconception: believes a negative irrational part cancels against a positive rational

options.text: The total is rational whenever t happens to be positive
options.misconception: believes adding a rational can absorb an irrational part when signs differ

options.text: The total is irrational for every irrational t
It depends on t with no rule connecting rational and irrational parts
options.misconception: believes irrationality is unpredictable rather than governed by closure rules

questions.explanation: Suppose 5 plus t came out rational; call it r. Then t would equal r minus 5, a difference of two rationals, which is rational, and that contradicts the choice of t. So 5 plus t must be irrational for every irrational t. The trap in B and C is imagining that a positive or negative irrational can be traded away against the whole number 5, but a rational plus an irrational never collapses to a single rational.
questions.hint: Assume the total is rational and see what that forces t to be.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: state when a rational multiplier preserves irrationality
questions.stem: A machine multiplies the irrational number the square root of 2 by a series of rational numbers. For which multipliers is the result guaranteed to be irrational?

options.text: Any positive rational, but negative multipliers can produce a rational
options.misconception: believes a negative multiplier can turn an irrational product into a rational

options.text: Any nonzero rational multiplier
Any rational except fractions, since fractions clear the radical
options.misconception: believes dividing an irrational by a whole number can remove the radical

options.text: Only whole-number multipliers, since rational factors behave differently
options.misconception: believes fractional multipliers behave differently from whole ones

questions.explanation: If c is a nonzero rational and c times the square root of 2 were rational, then dividing that rational by c would give the square root of 2 as a rational, which is impossible. So the product stays irrational for every nonzero rational c. The only multiplier that breaks the rule is 0, because 0 times any number is 0, a rational. Options B and D wrongly imagine that the sign or the form of the multiplier changes the logic, and C wrongly thinks a fraction can clear a radical.
questions.hint: Divide the product by the multiplier and see what you would get.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: predict whether a fraction terminates from its denominator
questions.stem: Four recipe measurements are written as fractions: 7 over 16, 3 over 14, 5 over 12, and 9 over 22. Which one has a decimal expansion that terminates?

options.text: 5 over 12, since the denominator ends in 2
options.misconception: believes a denominator ending in 2 always terminates the decimal

options.text: 3 over 14, since the denominator is small
options.misconception: believes a small denominator always gives a terminating decimal

options.text: 7 over 16, since 16 is a power of 2
9 over 22, since the denominator is composite
options.misconception: believes any composite denominator produces a terminating decimal

questions.explanation: A fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its reduced denominator has no prime factors besides 2 and 5. The denominator 16 is 2 to the fourth, so 7 over 16 equals 0.4375 and stops. The others fail: 14 carries a factor of 7, 12 carries a factor of 3, and 22 carries a factor of 11, so each long division eventually falls into a repeating cycle rather than running out of remainders.
questions.hint: Factor each denominator and keep only the primes 2 and 5.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: convert a two-digit repeating block to a fraction in lowest terms
questions.stem: A wheel turns 0.454545... with the block 45 repeating forever. Which fraction in lowest terms equals that number?

options.text: 45 over 100, because two repeating digits give two decimal places
options.misconception: treats a repeating block as if it were fixed decimal places

options.text: 45 over 99, which reduces to 5 over 11
5 over 10, because only the leading digit of the block repeats
options.misconception: believes only the first digit of a block repeats and the rest is noise

options.text: 45 over 999, because repeating decimals always use three nines
options.misconception: believes the denominator is 999 no matter how long the block is

questions.explanation: A block of n repeating digits becomes the block over a number made of n nines, so 0.454545... is 45 over 99, and dividing by 9 gives 5 over 11. The shortcut works because multiplying by 100 shifts one whole block left, and subtracting the original cancels the tail, leaving 99 times the value equal to 45. Option A is the trap of treating the repeat as a finite decimal, and D borrows a three-nines denominator that belongs to three-digit blocks.
questions.hint: Count the digits in one repeating block to choose the number of nines.

questions.learningObjective: compare a radical with a decimal by squaring both
questions.stem: Two running tracks are marked with lengths the square root of 10 metres and 3.2 metres. Which track is longer, and why?

options.text: The 3.2 metre track, since 3.2 squared is 10.24 and 10.24 is more than 10
The square root of 10 track, since radicals always beat decimal forms
options.misconception: believes any radical is automatically larger than any decimal

options.text: They are equal, since the square root of 10 rounds to 3.2
options.misconception: believes rounding to the same decimal makes two numbers equal

options.text: It cannot be decided without a calculator
options.misconception: believes comparing a radical with a decimal always needs a calculator

questions.explanation: Both values are positive, so comparing their squares compares the values: 3.2 squared is 10.24, which is greater than 10, so 3.2 is greater than the square root of 10 and that track is longer. Squaring is legitimate here because squaring preserves order among positive numbers. Option B is the reflexive belief that radicals are bigger, and C confuses rounding, which is an approximation, with exact equality.
questions.hint: Square both positive lengths and compare the results.

questions.learningObjective: deduce the classification of an unknown from an equation
questions.stem: A puzzle states that the square root of 2 plus some number r equals exactly 7. What can be concluded about r?

options.text: r is irrational, since a rational minus an irrational stays irrational
r is rational, since both numbers are lengths on the same ruler
options.misconception: believes numbers sharing a measuring context share a classification

options.text: r could be either, depending on how the square root of 2 is rounded
options.misconception: believes rounding an irrational part changes the exact classification

options.text: r equals 0, since the square root of 2 is smaller than 7
options.misconception: believes a smaller addend can be dropped when comparing sizes

questions.explanation: Rearranging gives r equal to 7 minus the square root of 2, and a rational minus an irrational is irrational, so r cannot be rational. The reasoning is the mirror image of the sum rule: if r were rational, then the sum of two rationals would be rational, yet the sum is 7. Rounding changes the written digits but never the exact value, so option C mistakes an approximation for the number itself.
questions.hint: Solve for r and check the class of each piece.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why an endless run of nines equals 1
questions.stem: A cash register shows a total of 0.99999 with the nines continuing forever, and the price tag says 1. Which claim about the two amounts is correct?

options.text: They are exactly equal, since both name the same point on the number line
The register total is always slightly less than 1, however many 9s appear
options.misconception: believes an infinitely repeated digit leaves a gap before the limit

options.text: They differ by 0.000...01, a number smaller than any decimal
options.misconception: believes a string of zeros can be infinite and still end in a digit

options.text: They are equal only in money, where values get rounded
options.misconception: believes the equality is a rounding convention rather than an exact fact

questions.explanation: Letting x be 0.999..., ten times x is 9.999..., and subtracting gives 9x equal to 9, so x equals 1 exactly. Equivalently, the difference 1 minus 0.999... is smaller than every positive number you can name, and the only such number is 0. Option B imagines a leftover gap at the end of an infinite process, and option C invents a final digit after infinitely many zeros, which cannot exist.
questions.hint: Multiply by 10 and subtract the original number.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: describe how many numbers lie between two rationals
questions.stem: Between the two rational numbers 1 over 3 and 1 over 2, a student claims there are only finitely many numbers. Which response is correct?

options.text: Infinitely many rationals sit between them, and infinitely many irrationals too
Exactly two numbers sit between them, one rational and one irrational
options.misconception: believes only one of each kind can fit between two fractions

options.text: Infinitely many rationals sit between them, but no irrationals do
options.misconception: believes irrationals cannot appear between two nearby rationals

options.text: No numbers sit between them, because both endpoints are fractions
options.misconception: believes fractions that are close together leave no room between

questions.explanation: The rationals are dense: the average of two rationals is a rational between them, so you can keep halving the remaining gap forever and never run out of rationals. Between any two different rationals there is also an irrational, for example the average plus a tiny irrational shift that keeps the value inside the interval. Option C is the tempting half-truth that density is a rational-only property, and D ignores that 1 over 3 is about 0.333 while 1 over 2 is 0.5, leaving room.
questions.hint: Average the two endpoints and ask what you get.

questions.learningObjective: classify a quotient of two irrationals
questions.stem: A surveyor writes a ramp slope as the square root of 8 divided by the square root of 2. Which statement about that quotient is correct?

options.text: It is irrational, because the radicands 8 and 2 are two different numbers
options.misconception: believes unequal radicands force an irrational quotient

options.text: It is irrational, because a quotient of two radicals is always irrational
options.misconception: assumes any quotient involving radicals stays irrational

options.text: It is rational, because every quotient of measured lengths is a fraction of whole numbers
options.misconception: believes all measurable quotients are automatically rational

options.text: It is rational, because the quotient simplifies to the square root of 4, which is 2

questions.explanation: Dividing the square root of 8 by the square root of 2 gives the square root of 8 over 2, which is the square root of 4, and that is exactly 2. Because 2 can be written as a fraction of integers, the quotient is rational. The trap is assuming that radicals always behave as irrationals, when simplifying first can reveal a whole number.
questions.hint: Rewrite the quotient as a single square root before deciding.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why no largest rational lies below an irrational
questions.stem: A student insists that 1.414 is the largest rational number that is still less than the square root of 2. Which response correctly refutes the claim?

options.misconception: believes longer decimals must overshoot rather than approach

options.text: The claim is right, since 1.414 is the closest three-place decimal to the root
options.misconception: believes a short truncation becomes the best possible rational bound

options.text: A larger rational exists, for example 1.4142, so there can be no largest one
The claim fails only because the root was rounded too early in the comparison

options.misconception: believes any endless decimal is automatically irrational

questions.stem: A steel beam is ordered at 3.2 metres, but the measured length is the square root of 10 metres. How much extra material is needed, to three decimal places?
questions.explanation: The square root of 10 is about 3.1623, so the shortfall is 3.2 minus 3.1623, which is about 0.0377 and rounds to 0.038. Because both lengths are positive, squaring them confirms the order, since 3.2 squared is 10.24 and that is larger than 10. The extra material is therefore the difference between the ordered size and the true size.

options.misconception: believes the numerator, not the reduced denominator, controls termination

options.text: The fraction is fine, because 24 divides 1000 and so the decimal has to stop
options.misconception: believes a large enough power of ten removes any denominator

The decimal repeats only because the learner reduced the fraction incorrectly
options.misconception: blames a valid reduction for the repeating pattern

questions.learningObjective: bracket a radical on a coarse number line

options.misconception: interpolates linearly in the radicands instead of comparing squares

options.text: The written decimal is rational, but the true ratio it estimates is irrational
The entry is rational, and the true ratio is rational too, since both name the same length

options.text: The true ratio is irrational, yet no decimal can ever stand close to it

options.text: The entry is irrational only because its digits are all below one thousand

options.text: A generating rule is not enough, since only a fixed repeating block makes a value rational

questions.explanation: A decimal is rational only when it terminates or settles into one fixed block that repeats forever, and here the runs of zeros keep growing, so no such block exists. A rule for writing digits gives no guarantee of rationality unless that rule produces a repeating block. Predictable growth is precisely what keeps this value irrational.
questions.hint: Ask whether the runs of zeros stay the same length forever.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: plot a four-place decimal on a coarse line
questions.stem: A number line is marked in tenths, and a point is plotted at 3.3166. Which statement about that point is correct?

options.text: It sits exactly on a mark, because 3.3166 rounds to 3.3
options.misconception: believes rounding to a mark moves the point onto it

options.text: It sits between 3.3 and 3.4 and represents the square root of 11
It sits between 3.4 and 3.5, because 11 is closer to 12.56 than to 10.89
options.misconception: misreads the squares of the neighbouring tenths

options.text: It cannot be plotted, because it is a decimal with four places
options.misconception: believes a line marked in tenths cannot carry finer values

questions.explanation: Since 3.3 squared is 10.89 and 3.4 squared is 11.56, the square root of 11, about 3.3166, lies between those marks. Rounding to the nearest tenth produces a label, not a position, and any value can be plotted by its coordinate regardless of the mark spacing. Finer values simply fall between the marks rather than on them.
questions.hint: Square 3.3 and 3.4 to bracket the value.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: report the longer of two lengths
questions.stem: A ladder reaches 3.9 metres and a beam is as long as the square root of 15 metres. Report the longer of the two lengths, to the nearest tenth of a metre.
questions.explanation: Squaring 3.9 gives 15.21, which is larger than 15, so the ladder is the longer of the two lengths. To the nearest tenth the ladder is 3.9 metres, while the beam is about 3.8730 metres and rounds to 3.9 as well. Comparing the squares is what identifies the winner before either value is rounded.
questions.hint: Square 3.9 and compare the result with 15.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: support the claim with a matching example pair
questions.stem: A student argues that multiplying two irrationals sometimes gives a rational and sometimes an irrational. Which pair of examples best supports that claim?

options.text: The square root of 2 with the square root of 3 gives the square root of 6, which simplifies to 1
options.misconception: misreads a product of radicals as a quotient of values

options.text: The square root of 2 with itself gives the square root of 4, which is nearly 2 but not exactly
options.misconception: doubts that a radical form can name an exact whole number

options.text: The square root of 2 with itself gives 2, while with the square root of 3 it gives the square root of 6
The square root of 2 with the square root of 8 gives the square root of 16, which is nearly 4
options.misconception: again treats an exact root as an approximation of itself

questions.explanation: Multiplying the square root of 2 by itself gives the square root of 4, which is exactly 2 and rational, while multiplying it by the square root of 3 gives the square root of 6, which stays irrational. The radicand product decides the outcome, so both cases genuinely occur. Options B and D wrongly suggest that a perfect square under a root is only approximate.
questions.hint: Multiply the radicands, then check whether the product is a perfect square.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: correct a count of values in a unit interval
questions.stem: A worksheet states that between any two consecutive whole numbers there are exactly nine numbers, one for each tenth. Which statement corrects it?

options.text: The count is wrong only because a whole unit really contains eleven tenths
options.misconception: fixes an arithmetic detail while missing the density claim

options.text: The count is right, because each whole unit contains one mark per tenth
options.misconception: believes marks at tenths exhaust the values between whole numbers

options.text: The count is right for the marks but wrong for the gaps between those marks
options.misconception: separates the marks from the numbers they label

options.text: There are infinitely many values in the gap, and the tenths are only a few of them

questions.explanation: Each unit interval contains infinitely many values, of which the tenths are only ten points. Even if only fractions are counted there are infinitely many, since one half, one third, one quarter and so on all land inside. Density means the gap is never exhausted by any finite set of marks.
questions.hint: Ask how many fractions of the form one over n lie between 0 and 1.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: state a rule true of every rational number
questions.stem: A statistician needs a statement that holds for every rational number. Which one qualifies?

options.text: Its decimal form must terminate, since a fraction is only a finite amount
options.misconception: believes every fraction ends rather than ever repeating

options.text: Its decimal form either terminates or settles into one fixed repeating block
Its decimal form must repeat, since every fraction has a cycle
options.misconception: believes every fraction repeats rather than ever terminating

options.text: Its value can always be written with exactly two digits after the point
options.misconception: believes a fixed number of decimal places can hold every rational

questions.explanation: Every rational equals a fraction of integers, and dividing the numerator by the denominator either ends with a remainder of zero or repeats a remainder, which fixes one block. So the decimal form terminates or repeats, and the two alternatives are not required together. Some fractions end, such as one eighth, and others repeat, such as one third.
questions.hint: Divide a fraction by hand and watch what happens to the remainders.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: select the strongest argument for the equality
questions.stem: A debate asks which argument best proves that 0.999 continuing forever equals 1. Which argument is the correct one?

options.text: The two values both sit nearer to 1 than to 0, so they are equal
options.misconception: believes sharing a proximity range makes two values equal

options.text: The two values round to the same number, so they must be equal
options.misconception: confuses a rounded display with an exact equality

options.text: Ten times the value minus the value leaves nine nines, which is exactly 9
The two values are both endless decimals, so they must be equal
options.misconception: believes a shared form of notation guarantees equal values

questions.explanation: Letting x stand for the endless decimal, ten times x is 9.999 continuing, and subtracting x leaves 9x equal to 9, so x is 1 exactly. Rounding and proximity describe how values look or sit, not whether they are equal, and two values sharing a form of notation can still differ. The subtraction argument settles the question by arithmetic alone.
questions.hint: Multiply by 10 and subtract the original value.
